waypoints.name: Dosewallips Road washout parking
waypoints.directions: From US 101 at Brinnon, turn west onto Dosewallips Road (FR 2610) at milepost 306, just north of Dosewallips State Park, and drive about 8.5 miles to where the road is closed to vehicles at the washout; park along the roadside. A Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass is required to park.

waypoints.name: Mount Constance summit
waypoints.directions: Walk or bike the closed road about 5 miles to the Lake Constance climbers' path and climb it about 2 miles to the lake. Head north up Avalanche Canyon past the Cat Ears and the mouth of the South Chute to the North Chute, the last major chute on the canyon's east side, and climb it to the ledge where the South Chute line joins. Cross the Finger Traverse (or the Terrible Traverse) and finish over the summit block.

approach_variants.name: Lake Constance climbers' trail, then up Avalanche Canyon past the South Chute
approach_variants.notes:
Bike or walk the closed Dosewallips Road (FS 2610) about 5 miles to the unsigned Lake Constance climbers' trail, then the steep, unmaintained trail roughly 3,300 ft in under 2.2 miles to Lake Constance at 4,800 ft. Camp at the north end of the lake.

From the lake, head north into Avalanche Canyon. This route is the parallel couloir further into the canyon: where the standard South Chute line turns east and climbs out early, the North Chute keeps you in the canyon bed longer and climbs from higher up it.

It sees less traffic than the South Chute and is commonly used as one half of a loop — up one, down the other — rather than as a route in its own right. It rejoins the standard line where the South Chute's gully tops out, crosses the Finger Traverse (or the Terrible Traverse when conditions allow), and finishes over the summit block and the North Chimney.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep. Snow in the chute is an improvement on the scree, but Avalanche Canyon is named for what runs down it in May and June
hazards: Avalanche hazard in Avalanche Canyon and its chutes is called out explicitly for May-June conditions
A long, loose gully with rockfall onto anyone below
It leads to the same exposed upper crossings as the standard route: the Finger Traverse ledge, or the Terrible Traverse's steep snow above a cliff
Less traffic means less boot track and fewer people to ask
approach_variants.baseFinding: The whole route-finding problem on this route is telling this chute from the other one, and the test is: keep walking up the canyon past the first chute. The published instruction for the South Chute is to start climbing east as soon as the Cat Ears tower is visible, and trip reports describing this line say plainly that you bypass the South Chute entrance and continue up loose talus to the mouth of the North Chute further into Avalanche Canyon. So the discriminator is temporal, not visual: the first opportunity to leave the canyon eastward is the wrong one. In cloud, where the Cat Ears cannot be seen at all, this is still workable because the test is about the canyon floor under your feet rather than about a skyline. From the lake, follow the canyon north. Do not turn uphill at the first gully. Keep going on the talus until the canyon delivers you to a second, more northerly couloir, and take that. The confirming test is at the top of the chute: it narrows and eases, and the summit block comes into sight to the north for the first time. Just above, a narrow exposed ledge trending left meets the point where the South Chute's loose gully comes in from below. From there the two routes are the same line: north through a notch, across a snowfield, then the Finger Traverse (a downsloping ledge with a horizontal finger crack and old pitons), or the lower Terrible Traverse, the steep exposed snow crossing above a large cliff, when conditions allow. Honest limit: this chute is documented mostly as a variation inside other parties' loops. It is long, loose and less travelled, and there is no marker sequence inside the gully itself.

approach_variants.name: Dosewallips road and Constance Pass, over Crystal Pass into upper Avalanche Canyon
approach_variants.notes: The alternative that avoids the Lake Constance trail. Road-walk or bike roughly 6.5 miles from the washout past the Lake Constance turn-off to the road end at the old campground and ranger station, then the Constance Pass Trail south and southwest to Constance Pass at about 5,850 ft. Leave the trail, travel cross-country west into the head of Crystal Basin, and climb to Crystal Pass on the Constance-Warrior massif. From Crystal Pass drop south into upper Avalanche Canyon. This is the variant that suits this route best of the three Constance routes, because the North Chute is the higher of the two chutes and coming in from Crystal Pass you meet it without walking the whole canyon up from the lake.
hazards: Unmarked cross-country between Constance Pass and Crystal Pass on talus, scree and lingering snow
No water above Constance Pass except transient snowmelt
Avalanche and rockfall in the canyon and the chute
Commits to the exposed Finger or Terrible Traverse at the end of a long approach day
Roughly 6.5 miles of closed road at each end
approach_variants.baseFinding:
This is the one approach where the North Chute is the easy one to find, because you arrive above it. Dropping into Avalanche Canyon from Crystal Pass on the intermittent climbers' path, the first couloir that offers a line up onto the Constance side is the North Chute. Take it. If you keep descending the canyon you will next pass the Cat Ears and the Thumb and eventually reach the South Chute entrance and then the lake — every one of which means you have gone below the route.

The confirming test is the same as on the lake approach: near its top the chute narrows and eases, the summit block comes into sight to the north, and a narrow exposed ledge trending left meets the point where the South Chute's gully joins from below. Above that the line is shared with the standard route and crosses the Finger Traverse, or the Terrible Traverse when conditions allow.

Honest limit: the climbers' track fades near Crystal Pass, so this variant's own approach is the navigationally hard part, not the chute.
